units.title: Unit 45 — Taste and smell
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 94–95 (PDF pages 98–99).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Basic concepts · taste, smell and figurative senses
learningObjectives: Use natural positive collocations for scents, aromas and flavours in food and travel descriptions.
Distinguish negative smell and taste expressions by intensity, meaning and register.
Use verbs and set phrases for testing food, noticing odours and describing stale products.
Recognise figurative taste and smell expressions for impressions, preferences and suspected danger.

items.example: The fragrant perfume of the orange blossom filled the courtyard.
items.note: Fragrant describes a pleasant sweet or delicate smell; perfume can refer poetically to flowers as well as to a product.

items.example: The tea has a distinctive aroma that I recognise immediately.
items.note: Distinctive means easily recognisable and different from other smells, particularly of food and drink.

items.example: A rich aroma of roasted nuts drifted through the bakery.
items.note: Rich suggests a deep, full and often pleasant aroma.

items.example: The strong aroma of spices reached the hallway.
items.note: Strong intensifies aroma without necessarily saying it is unpleasant.

items.example: A sweet aroma rose from the warm cinnamon buns.
items.note: Sweet can describe an odour reminiscent of sugar or sweet flowers.

items.example: An appetising aroma came from the soup simmering on the stove.
items.note: Appetising means the smell makes you want to eat.

items.example: The delicious aroma of fresh bread greeted us at the door.
items.note: Delicious can describe an inviting food smell, not just its taste.

items.example: The smell of fresh coffee spread through the kitchen.
items.note: Smell is the neutral everyday noun for an odour; of introduces what produces it.

items.pt: fragrância fresca; cheiro fresco e agradável
items.example: A fresh scent of rosemary filled the greenhouse.
items.note: Scent is often used for pleasant or recognisable smells, particularly plants and perfume.

items.example: The fresh scent of herbs surrounded us in the garden.
items.note: The phrase describes the pleasant smell associated with newly picked or growing herbs.

items.pt: gosto adquirido; algo de que se aprende a gostar
items.example: Black olives can be an acquired taste for young children.
items.note: An acquired taste is something you may dislike initially but come to enjoy over time.

items.example: The sauce has a subtle flavour of lemon.
items.note: Subtle indicates a taste that is delicate and not immediately obvious.

items.example: Subtle flavours of thyme and garlic make the dish interesting.
items.note: Use subtle for gentle, hard-to-identify flavours rather than intense ones.

items.example: Plain rice is a perfect accompaniment to this spicy curry.
items.note: Accompaniment names something, often a side dish, that goes well with another food.

items.word: the aroma of cinnamon wafts across the room
items.pt: o aroma de canela se espalha suavemente pela sala
items.example: The aroma of cinnamon wafts across the room whenever we bake biscuits.
items.note: Waft suggests gentle movement of a smell through the air, rather than an abrupt burst.

items.word: the smell of toast wafts in from the kitchen
items.pt: o cheiro de torrada vem suavemente da cozinha
items.example: The smell of toast wafts in from the kitchen every morning.
items.note: Waft in describes a smell entering a place gently; often followed by from to name its origin.

items.example: I prefer bitter coffee without sugar.
items.note: Bitter describes an unsweet, sharp taste; it is not the same as sour.

items.example: Milk can go sour if it is left outside the fridge.
items.note: Go sour describes food, especially dairy products, becoming acidic or spoiled.

items.example: We had to throw away the sour milk.
items.note: Sour describes an acidic taste or smell; with milk it usually suggests spoilage.

items.example: Acrid smoke from the burning plastic made everyone cough.
items.note: Acrid is sharp and unpleasant, often irritating the throat or nose.

items.example: Workers wore masks because the paint released noxious fumes.
items.note: Noxious describes gases or fumes that are harmful or poisonous; fumes is normally plural.

items.example: The containers held foul-smelling chemicals.
items.note: Foul-smelling is strongly negative and usually describes a disgusting odour.

items.example: Residents complained about a foul-smelling factory beside the river.
items.note: The compound adjective describes something emitting an offensive smell.

items.example: Body odour became more noticeable in the crowded changing room.
items.note: Body odour usually refers to the smell caused by sweat; British spelling is odour.

items.pt: amargo demais para o meu gosto
items.example: That dark chocolate is too bitter for my taste.
items.note: For my taste expresses personal preference; here bitter refers to actual flavour.

items.section: C · Describing and testing smells and tastes
items.example: A strong smell of garlic remained in the kitchen.
items.note: Strong is neutral about how pleasant a smell is; context supplies the evaluation.

items.section: C · Describing and testing smells and tastes
items.example: Have a taste of the stew before you add more salt.
items.note: Have a taste invites someone to sample a small quantity of food or drink.

items.section: C · Describing and testing smells and tastes
items.example: Have a smell of these flowers and tell me what you think.
items.note: Have a smell is an informal way of inviting someone to smell something.

items.section: C · Describing and testing smells and tastes
items.example: The fish smells off, so we should not cook it.
items.note: Off describes food that no longer smells fresh; it is not about being switched off.

items.pt: um fedor insuportável; um mau cheiro muito forte
items.section: C · Describing and testing smells and tastes
items.example: An overpowering stink came from the blocked drain.
items.note: Overpowering emphasises that an unpleasant smell is extremely strong.

items.pt: exalar um cheiro; emitir um odor
items.section: C · Describing and testing smells and tastes
items.example: The damp carpet gives off a smell after heavy rain.
items.note: Give off means release or emit a smell, heat or light; it does not mean remove it.

items.pt: um fedor repugnante; um mau cheiro nauseante
items.section: C · Describing and testing smells and tastes
items.example: A revolting stench came from the abandoned rubbish bags.
items.note: Stench is stronger and more extreme than stink; revolting adds a sense of disgust.

items.pt: perceber um leve cheiro de perfume
items.section: C · Describing and testing smells and tastes
items.example: I could detect a whiff of perfume as she passed.
items.note: Detect means notice a faint trace; a whiff is a brief or slight smell.

items.section: C · Describing and testing smells and tastes
items.example: A whiff of perfume lingered near the doorway.
items.note: A whiff is much less intense than an overpowering smell.

items.pt: deixar um leve rastro de perfume
items.section: C · Describing and testing smells and tastes
items.example: She left a whiff of perfume in the lift.
items.note: Leave a whiff suggests a slight lingering scent after someone has passed.

items.word: leave a bad taste in your mouth
items.pt: deixar uma sensação ruim; deixar um gosto amargo
items.example: The way the manager treated the staff left a bad taste in my mouth.
items.note: Figuratively means an unpleasant impression remains after an experience, not a physical taste.

items.word: leave an unpleasant taste in your mouth
items.pt: deixar uma impressão desagradável; deixar um gosto amargo
items.example: The rude exchange left an unpleasant taste in my mouth.
items.note: A close figurative alternative to leave a bad taste in your mouth; not literally about eating.

items.example: After years of strict rules, she finally tasted freedom.
items.note: Taste is figurative: to experience a welcome or unfamiliar state.

items.word: share the same taste in music
items.example: My sister and I share the same taste in music.
items.note: Taste in refers to preferences; the same pattern works with films, art and clothes.

items.pt: desenvolver gosto por; passar a gostar de
items.example: He developed a taste for spicy food while travelling.
items.note: Develop a taste for means gradually start to enjoy an activity, food or style.

items.example: The hikers smelt danger when the weather suddenly changed.
items.note: Figuratively means sense that something risky may happen; smelt is British past tense.

items.pt: captar o espírito de; ter uma ideia geral de
items.example: The short video helps visitors get the flavour of local life.
items.note: Figuratively means grasp the character or general idea of something rather than the details.

units.title: Unit 46 — Number and frequency
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 96–97 (PDF pages 100–101).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Basic concepts · quantity, counts, frequency and trends
learningObjectives: Combine quantity adjectives accurately with number or amount to express degree and importance.
Describe numerical changes and totals using appropriate noun and verb patterns.
Discuss repeated events and the spread or rarity of phenomena with natural collocations.
Describe chart trends, changes in rates and stable values using accurate adverbs and nouns.

items.section: A · Commenting on how much or how many
items.example: Even a minute amount of dye can colour the water.
items.note: Minute is pronounced /maɪˈnjuːt/ here and means extremely small, not sixty seconds.

items.section: A · Commenting on how much or how many
items.example: Add a tiny amount of salt to the sauce.
items.note: Tiny emphasises very small quantity; with an uncountable substance use amount.

items.pt: um número muito pequeno; pouquíssimas pessoas ou coisas
items.section: A · Commenting on how much or how many
items.example: Only a tiny number of applicants had the required experience.
items.note: Use number with countable people or things; of introduces the group.

items.section: A · Commenting on how much or how many
items.example: The company invested a significant amount of money in training.
items.note: Significant suggests importance or a quantity large enough to matter, not merely a big size.

items.section: A · Commenting on how much or how many
items.example: A significant number of students chose online classes.
items.note: Significant stresses that the count is meaningful or important, even if not a majority.

items.section: A · Commenting on how much or how many
items.example: A surprising number of visitors arrived despite the rain.
items.note: Surprising expresses an unexpected count rather than necessarily a large one.

items.section: A · Commenting on how much or how many
items.example: The repair required a surprising amount of effort.
items.note: Amount goes with uncountable nouns; surprising signals an unexpected degree.

items.section: A · Commenting on how much or how many
items.example: She spent a considerable amount of time preparing the talk.
items.note: Considerable means fairly large in scale; this is common in formal descriptions.

items.section: A · Commenting on how much or how many
items.example: A considerable number of residents attended the meeting.
items.note: Number refers to countable items or people; it often suggests an appreciable group.

items.section: A · Commenting on how much or how many
items.example: The company has raised a substantial amount of funding.
items.note: Substantial suggests a large, important or solidly measurable quantity.

items.pt: um número expressivo; um número considerável
items.section: A · Commenting on how much or how many
items.example: A substantial number of passengers missed the connection.
items.note: Substantial conveys a large or meaningful number; avoid translating it as physical substance.

items.section: A · Commenting on how much or how many
items.example: They collected an enormous amount of data during the study.
items.note: Enormous marks an extremely large quantity and can be more emphatic than substantial.

items.section: A · Commenting on how much or how many
items.example: An enormous number of people watched the final.
items.note: Use number, not amount, for countable people or things.

items.section: A · Commenting on how much or how many
items.example: A relatively small number of users reported the issue.
items.note: Relatively compares a count with a larger reference group without claiming it is unimportant.

items.example: Seven and eleven are odd numbers.
items.note: Odd means not divisible by two; it does not mean strange in this mathematical phrase.

items.example: Twelve and fourteen are even numbers.
items.note: Even means divisible by two; it contrasts with odd in number classification.

items.word: a decline in the number of
items.pt: uma redução no número de; uma queda no número de
items.example: A decline in the number of accidents followed the safety campaign.
items.note: Decline is relatively formal and often describes a downward numerical trend.

items.word: a drop in the number of
items.example: There was a drop in the number of late deliveries this month.
items.note: Drop is a more informal alternative to decline; retain the preposition in.

items.word: an increase in the number of
items.example: An increase in the number of requests put pressure on the team.
items.note: Use increase in with the quantity that changes, rather than increase of the number.

items.word: a rise in the number of
items.pt: uma elevação no número de; um aumento no número de
items.example: A rise in the number of bookings surprised the staff.
items.note: Rise is often slightly less formal than increase for an upward count.

items.example: All the expenses come to a total of £320.
items.note: An amount or calculation comes to a total; the person doing the calculation arrives at one.

items.example: After counting every ticket, we arrived at a total of 480.
items.note: The person calculating arrives at a total; figures themselves come to a total.

items.example: The birth rate rises when the number of births grows relative to the population.
items.note: A rate may rise, fall, drop or decline; the change is in the rate, not necessarily the total population.

items.example: The birth rate falls when fewer babies are born per thousand residents.
items.note: Falls is the natural intransitive verb: do not say the rate lowers in this sense.

items.example: The birth rate declines over several years in the forecast.
items.note: Declines can sound more formal or gradual than falls.

items.example: The pound is a unit of currency used in the United Kingdom.
items.note: Currency refers to money used in an economic system, not an individual banknote.

items.example: The metre is a standard unit of measurement for length.
items.note: Measurement names the process or standard of quantifying something.

items.example: The energy bill lists the cost per unit of electricity.
items.note: A unit of electricity is a billing quantity, commonly measured in kilowatt-hours.

items.example: A centimetre is a unit of length.
items.note: Unit of length specifies the physical dimension being measured.

items.pt: a taxa de desemprego está caindo
items.example: The latest report says the unemployment rate is falling.
items.note: Use fall with an intransitive rate; lowering would need an agent and an object in a different structure.

items.example: The discovery attracted widespread interest among researchers.
items.note: Widespread indicates interest shared across many people or groups.

items.example: The new recycling programme gained widespread support.
items.note: Widespread describes broad distribution of support, not necessarily unanimous agreement.

items.example: The flood caused widespread damage across the region.
items.note: Widespread focuses on damage across many places; it is not the same as severe damage.

items.example: The charity works in areas affected by widespread poverty.
items.note: Widespread means occurring among many people or in many places.

items.example: The proposal faced widespread criticism from local residents.
items.note: Widespread can describe negative reactions as well as support or interest.

items.example: Researchers are studying treatments for rare diseases.
items.note: Rare describes low prevalence; a rare disease may still be serious.

items.example: The birdwatchers spotted a rare bird near the lake.
items.note: Rare refers to a species or sighting that is uncommon.

items.example: The protected area is home to several rare species.
items.note: Species has the same form in singular and plural; rare describes scarcity.

items.example: The collector displayed several rare coins.
items.note: Rare is used for scarce objects valued by collectors, not just natural species.

items.example: My colleagues keep asking when the new system will be ready.
items.note: Keep plus the -ing form expresses repeated action, often with annoyance in informal speech.

items.example: Please do not keep interrupting the speaker.
items.note: Keep interrupting signals repeated interruptions and often frustration.

items.example: They keep promising improvements without announcing a date.
items.note: Keep plus -ing often suggests repetition that the speaker finds frustrating.

items.example: Constant interruptions made the meeting unproductive.
items.note: Constant highlights repeated or seemingly uninterrupted occurrences.

items.example: His continual complaining spoiled the atmosphere.
items.note: Continual describes repeated behaviour over time, not necessarily literally without pauses.

items.example: Sales rose sharply after the product launch.
items.note: Sharply indicates a large or sudden increase, often shown by a steep line on a graph.

items.pt: subir rapidamente; subir de forma acentuada
items.example: Demand rose steeply during the first week.
items.note: Steeply highlights the sharp slope of a rise when describing data.

items.example: Passenger numbers fell sharply in January.
items.note: Fall is intransitive and sharply marks a rapid downward change.

items.pt: cair vertiginosamente; cair de forma acentuada
items.example: Prices fell steeply when supply recovered.
items.note: Steeply conveys the size and steep slope of a decline.

items.pt: um aumento expressivo; uma alta acentuada
items.example: The chart shows a dramatic rise in online orders.
items.note: Dramatic stresses that an increase is notably large or striking.

items.pt: uma queda acentuada; uma redução drástica
items.example: There was a dramatic fall in energy consumption after the upgrade.
items.note: Fall is a noun here and combines with the adjective dramatic.

items.example: Output increased steadily throughout the quarter.
items.note: Steadily means at a consistent rate or without major interruptions, not necessarily quickly.

items.example: The water temperature increased gradually during the test.
items.note: Gradually focuses on a slow progression over time.

items.example: The current remained constant during the measurement.
items.note: Constant indicates the measured value did not change appreciably.

items.example: Prices remained stable for three months.
items.note: Stable means little variation, not necessarily a perfectly unchanging value.

items.pt: um aumento contínuo; uma elevação constante
items.example: There was a steady rise in attendance over the summer.
items.note: Steady rise describes an ongoing, relatively even increase; it contrasts with a sudden spike.

items.example: The study reports a steady decline in traffic injuries.
items.note: Steady decline describes a consistent downward pattern without major fluctuations.

items.example: There has been a steady fall in fuel consumption since April.
items.note: Steady fall and steady decline have similar meanings, although decline can sound more formal.

items.example: The incidence of disease fell after the vaccination programme.
items.note: Incidence measures new cases over a period; here it is used as the quantity undergoing change.
